items.title: Winners and losers from Austria MotoGP sprint 2026
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
The Austrian Grand Prix MotoGP sprint race seemed to have a nailed-on winner until three laps to go when that rider made an inexplicable mistake.

So that’s one slot in our list below decided very easily…

Loser: Pedro Acosta (DNF)

Acosta had this race completely in the bag when he blew the chicane so comprehensively he was sliding through the run-off area on his side.

Credit to him for so readily admitting that he “just f***ed it up”. But also Pedro… you’re supposed to be an era-defining superstar, don’t f**k up obvious race-winning opportunities. Next year that will be very, very costly.

Winner: Jorge Martin (1st)

Every time you feel like you can rule Martin out of something in 2026, there he is again. Often leading the championship, and for a long time doing so by a lot more points than seems logical for his actual pace.

So it was probably predictable he’d follow the Misano arm pump and championship lead loss with a performance like this. He didn’t really look like a Red Bull Ring pole contender until there he was suddenly on pole. And even if Acosta hadn’t crashed, going from eighth to second after his first lap incident and outperforming his main title rivals with such apparent ease would have already been a huge warning shot to them.

This season clearly has a few twists in it yet, and Martin will probably be at the centre of them all.

Losers: Martin's title rivals (2nd & 3rd)

Second and third was kind of fine for Marc Marquez and Marco Bezzecchi - especially Marquez. Bezzecchi really needs to be clawing some big handfuls of points back from his rivals to have any title hope now but at least didn't lose too much today, Marquez really needn’t worry about being three points behind Martin again tonight having already come back from being 85 behind him once this season.

But given they’re in a championship fight, Martin sliced past both Bezzecchi and Marquez a little too easily for comfort today.

Ogura had expected very little from his first weekend back from finger injury - to run in the 11th-12th range, to be precise - but he's looked totally in the groove, and with no particular physical limitation to speak of.

At 77 points adrift the championship train has left the station, but at least there's no sign at all of Ogura's campaign being derailed by mid-year disruption the way it was last year.

Loser: Raul Fernandez (19th)

Both Fernandez and LCR Honda rider Diogo Moreira had their sprint undone by penalties for jumping the start, both seemingly caught out by the red lights being on a little longer than is conventional. Fernandez was confused by the sanction, but Moreira held up his hand.

And while Moreira at least has something to be happy about, having improved his situation through the twisty third sector, Fernandez remains at sea. It is now the third round in a row that he doesn't look quite right, and he says the feeling of rear grip hasn't been quite right in all three.

It's left Fernandez "worried" going forward, particularly for tracks with more of a stop-start layout - of which the next round at Motegi is also one.

Winner: Pecco Bagnaia (6th)

Bagnaia looked like he'd rather be anywhere else on Earth when he rocked up to his media debrief after a dreadful Friday. On Saturday, he was all smiles and jokes - even if he's had plenty of better MotoGP finishes than this one.

Some overnight tweaks to find badly-needed rear grip finally paid off, and he banked crucial prep for Sunday by running the medium rear tyre in the sprint. 

And after having put Spanish broadcaster DAZN on blast coming into the weekend, he was grateful to one person in their staff. That person? Pundit (and KTM tester) Dani Pedrosa, who said Bagnaia needs to focus on feeling on the bike and totally ignore the timesheets - advice that Bagnaia says he has taken to heart.

Losers: Yamaha riders (17th, 18th, 20th) who aren't Fabio Quartararo (12th)

For a second successive weekend, coming off his PR explosion versus Yamaha leadership at Aragon, Quartararo is riding absolute circles around his M1 peers. Stablemate Jack Miller described his Q2 laptime here - a second clear of the other Yamahas - as a "miracle".

It was the same amount of points for each of them, i.e. no points - but Quartararo clearly dug in for his 12th place in the sprint, while his peers all couldn't hide their frustration: Alex Rins admitting it stung to be stuck behind Honda test rider Taka Nakagami, Toprak Razgatlioglu was irritated by the battle antics of another test rider Pol Espargaro, and Miller as angry as he's been all season about a lack of a workable electronics set-up.

Winner: Johann Zarco (7th)

Speaking of lone warriors carrying their manufacturer forward… well, OK, Zarco’s margin over the other Hondas is not quite in Quartararo/other Yamahas territory, and admittedly Joan Mir is absent.

But in making it to Q2 (over three tenths of a second clear of LCR team-mate Moreira and works rider Luca Marini) and then sticking with the Alex Marquez-led group in the race on the way to seventh while next-best Honda Marini was six places and 10 seconds further back, Zarco was definitely the only rider saving Honda honour today.

That’s the best actual race finish since he returned from his savage Barcelona injury, though he’s slipped so comfortably back into regular top 10 running that it doesn’t even seem that exceptional. And he thinks his full-distance race pace tomorrow is likely to be better too.

Loser: Fabio Di Giannantonio (10th)

The 'Di Giannantonio title challenge' balloon has continued its inexorable deflation here, as the VR46 rider lost crucial ground on the opening lap - at Turn 1, Turn 3 and Turn 4 - and couldn't recover to the points.

This is not Ducati's strongest weekend, obviously, but Di Giannantonio had looked in a better position within the Ducati ranks on Friday than on Saturday - and it's been a long, long while since he's been the clear standout among the Desmosedicis.

The rider who will effectively inherit his seat next year, Fermin Aldeguer, also performed below his Friday baseline - but at least made some moves and got some points.

items.title: Who actually owns each F1 team?
items.author: Darren Cox
items.content:
Who is benefiting from the huge spike in Formula 1 team valuations? While writing my recent piece on why team valuations are ramping up so fast, I realised that I didn’t definitively know that answer for each team. 

With the interest in valuations, plus the ongoing story around Cadillac’s ownership and recent revelations around Aston Martin shareholding I thought I’d go down some rabbit holes and look into available shareholding information for each team. 

Available is a key word here. Depending on the type of ownership structure and where it is domiciled the strength and depth of the information differs. 

The answer to the seemingly simple question of ‘Who actually owns each F1 team’ is actually very complex. Having dug deep and thought about how we got here, there are three key reasons for people to want to own part of an F1 team. Those reasons do overlap but have undeniably shifted since the ‘owner/operator’ models of Frank Williams, Colin Chapman, Bruce McLaren and Ken Tyrrell when the only target was to win. 

1) You own one because you want to go racing. 

2) You own one because going racing helps another business make money. 

3) You (part) own one because you believe the racing team itself will make you money.

Frank Williams largely represented the first. Benetton and Red Bull are examples of the second. The arrival of Arctos, Otro and other institutional investors represents the third.

But we are not anywhere close to a grid with a 100% ownership by institutional investors, representing reason 3. And that’s what makes the detail so interesting. 

Today's grid is increasingly populated by hybrids. Manufacturers alongside private capital, billionaire controllers alongside institutional investors, sovereign wealth alongside entrepreneurs, even senior employees owning equity. 

Once you dig into these structures some of the strategic decisions of the teams and cultural differences make sense. Gene Haas is the only 100% owner/operator left on the grid. Haas are also the only team operating below the cost cap. This is perhaps not a surprise correlation.

With Haas being the simplest to explain, I’ll start at the opposite end of the complexity scale.

Aston Martin: Lawrence Stroll controls it, but plenty of others own part of it

Stroll doesn't simply 'own' Aston Martin F1, and Aston Martin Lagonda, the listed road car company whose name is above the door, doesn't own the F1 team either.

The F1 business ultimately sits within AMR GP Holdings Limited and this is probably the best example on the grid of how sophisticated F1 ownership has become.

PlanetF1 recently did some detailed digging into filings relating to Adrian Newey's shareholding and calculated that Stroll-related interests account for around a third of the economic ownership of the team. 

It also highlighted something considerably more important: Stroll doesn't need to own anything close to a majority to control it.

UK Companies House currently records Racing Point UK Holdings Limited, the Stroll-led consortium holding vehicle, as owning more than 25% but no more than 50% of AMR GP Holdings' shares. But it has 75% or more of the voting rights and the right to appoint or remove directors.

Then it gets more interesting.

The latest articles of association define Racing Point UK Holdings as the 'Controlling Shareholder' for as long as it owns at least 15% of the company's shares.

That status brings significant governance rights, including around appointment of the chairman, directors and the quorum required for board meetings.

So Stroll has achieved something increasingly important in modern F1, he has brought substantial amounts of other people's capital into the business, and crystallised some of the extraordinary increase in its value, without surrendering control.

Arctos Partners, one of the biggest specialist sports investment firms in the world, is a substantial shareholder. HPS Investment Partners is another. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has an interest. Woody Johnson, owner of the New York Jets, joined through Delaware vehicle Green Racer LLC. Adrian Newey has an equity interest through a special class of shares. There are also management interests.

PlanetF1's analysis puts Newey's interest at approximately 4.7% and Racing Point UK itself at around 27%, with total Stroll-associated interests around 33%.

Ferrari: Publicly owned, family influenced

Ferrari ought to be straightforward as well.

It isn't a separately syndicated F1 operation like Aston Martin. Scuderia Ferrari sits inside Ferrari itself.

And Ferrari is a publicly listed company, so in one sense it has thousands of owners.

But that doesn't mean all Ferrari shares are created equally when it comes to control.

As of February 2026, Exor, the Agnelli family's investment company, owned 21.33% of Ferrari's ordinary shares.

Thanks to Ferrari's loyalty voting structure, those shares represented 32.32% of the voting power.

Piero Ferrari's trust held another 10.67% economically, representing 16.17% of the votes.

Put those together and interests representing around 32% of the economic ownership command approximately 48.5% of the voting power..

So saying Ferrari is ‘publicly owned’ is correct.

Saying Ferrari is a company over which the Agnelli/Exor and Ferrari family interests retain enormous influence is also correct.

And this is a good example of the difference between economic ownership and control.

There is another important difference with Ferrari. If someone says the Ferrari F1 team is worth $5billion, there isn't a standalone company containing Scuderia Ferrari that can simply be bought for that number.

Ferrari's F1 team is part of the wider Ferrari business.

That makes comparing an implied Ferrari F1 valuation with, say, a transaction in Aston Martin or Alpine slightly more apples and pears than most valuation tables acknowledge.

Red Bull and Racing Bulls: Two F1 teams, one strategic purpose

At its simplest, Red Bull Racing and Racing Bulls are ultimately part of the Red Bull empire.

This is perhaps the best current example of our second reason for owning an F1 team: going racing helps another business make money.

Red Bull wasn't created to go motor racing. Red Bull Racing was created to help sell Red Bull.

That has worked rather well.

But the ownership trail is worth understanding.

At the UK level, Red Bull Technology sits above much of the Milton Keynes operation. Companies House currently identifies Mark Mateschitz as owning more than 25% but no more than 50% of Red Bull Technology. The same pattern runs through Red Bull Powertrains and other UK entities.

Ultimately, however, you arrive at privately-held Austrian parent Red Bull GmbH and the interests of the Mateschitz and Yoovidhya families.

That structure has itself changed since Dietrich Mateschitz's death and there has been a further change involving a 2% holding previously held personally by Chalerm Yoovidhya being transferred to Swiss trustee Fides Trustees.

Mercedes: Three equal owners, plus one

Mercedes is refreshingly easy at team level.

Mercedes-Benz, INEOS (ultimately Sir Jim Ratcliffe) and Toto Wolff each own one third.

When INEOS joined the ownership in 2020, Mercedes explicitly announced that the team would be owned in three equal parts. Companies House still identifies Mercedes-Benz Holdings UK, INEOS Industries Holdings and Toto Wolff as the three active persons/entities with significant control.

Except there is now a footnote.

Because that entity owns one third of Mercedes, Kurtz's indirect economic interest is equivalent to around 5% of the F1 team.

Crucially, Mercedes said the governance had not changed. Wolff remains in control of his ownership entity and continues as CEO and team principal, although Kurtz joined the team's strategic steering committee alongside Wolff, Ola Källenius (Mercedes) and Ratcliffe.

This is a small transaction but an interesting one.

Wolff has effectively been able to sell part of his economic exposure to an F1 team valued in the billions without giving up his position or changing the three-way governance structure.

McLaren: Sovereign capital has ended up owning the racing team

McLaren's ownership has recently become simpler.

During the pandemic, McLaren Racing brought in MSP Sports Capital and other investors at a time when the wider McLaren organisation badly needed capital.

That proved to be a spectacular investment.

In September 2025 McLaren announced that the remaining minority shareholders MSP, O'Connor Capital Solutions, Ares and Caspian had been bought out.

That left Bahrain's Mumtalakat and Abu Dhabi-based CYVN Holdings owning 100% of McLaren Racing between them.

Mumtalakat remains the majority shareholder and CYVN holds a non-controlling stake. McLaren has not publicly disclosed the exact split.

The transaction reportedly valued McLaren Racing at more than $4billion.

This is an important distinction from McLaren Automotive, which has gone through its own ownership restructuring. McLaren Racing is the business we are interested in here, and it contains more than F1. IndyCar and McLaren's incoming World Endurance Championship programme also sit within the racing operation.

Again, what exactly are we valuing when we say ‘McLaren F1 is worth $4billion’?

It isn't necessarily only the two orange cars turning up at 24 grands prix.

Cadillac: The newest team produces one of the least obvious answers

If you asked somebody who owns the Cadillac F1 team, the instinctive answer would probably be General Motors.

Formula 1 itself described the successful entry application as being made by General Motors and TWG Motorsports, and TWG CEO Dan Towriss has subsequently confirmed publicly that GM is an equity owner in the team

But the UK corporate record gives us another name.

The British company is now TWG Cadillac Formula 1 Team Limited.

Companies House identifies Mark Walter as its sole active person with significant control, on the basis that he “has significant influence or control”.

TWG is Walter's wider investment group and its sports interests stretch well beyond Formula 1. With Walter very recently and unexpectedly selling parts of his sports investment portfolio including the LA Lakers and Chelsea FC, facing increasing US government scrutiny and with MSP (see McLaren above) principals spotted in the Cadillac motorhome during the Madrid F1 weekend, the longevity of TWG involvement in F1 is currently in doubt. 

TWG itself recently denied reports that those assets might be for sale.

So where exactly does GM sit economically?

Public descriptions variously refer to TWG owning the team in partnership with GM or to a TWG owned operation backed by GM. What isn't publicly available is a clean percentage split. Paddock insiders suggest that GM has options up to 30%, Dan Towriss has 3% with Walter owning the remaining equity.

Audi: A works team with a sovereign wealth shareholder

Audi is another good example of the modern hybrid.

Audi initially moved to take complete ownership of Sauber Holding as it prepared for its 2026 works entry.

Then, before the Audi name had even appeared on an F1 grid, Qatar Investment Authority signed definitive agreements to acquire a significant minority stake in Sauber Holding.

Neither Audi nor QIA publicly disclosed the final percentage in their announcement. Formula 1 described it as a “substantial minority” investment and a significant capital injection into the project.

Subsequently Audi has admitted to various parties including Joe Saward to be looking towards a Mercedes-esque split, looking at offers for 33% of the team in part a reaction to cost cutting and major restructuring within the wider VW group. 

Alpine: Renault owns 76%, financial investors own 24%

After some of the structures above, Alpine almost feels straightforward, despite being the most newsworthy in recent months. 

Renault Group owns 76% of Alpine Racing Limited.

An investor group led by Otro Capital owns 24%.

The latter stake was acquired for €200million in 2023, valuing Alpine Racing at around $900million at the time. Renault explicitly identified Otro, RedBird Capital Partners and Maximum Effort Investments as the investor group.

The investment subsequently attracted plenty of headlines because athletes and celebrities including Patrick Mahomes, Rory McIlroy and others participated.

But the important ownership point is that Renault retained very clear legal and voting control. Its 76% holding also puts it above the 75% threshold required for major corporate decisions such as special resolutions under UK company law.

Williams: An F1 team owned as an investment

Williams is historically important to this story because for decades it was almost the definition of our first ownership model.

Frank Williams owned a racing team (with Patrick Head) because he wanted to race. The only blip in the simple model was a long forgotten part listing on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and a cameo role from Toto Wolff (with 15% equity). This was a glimpse of the hybrid ownership model we now see over a decade later. 

The modern Williams represents something very different.

Dorilton Capital acquired Williams in August 2020 following the strategic review undertaken by the then-listed Williams business. Williams described Dorilton at the time as a US-headquartered private investment firm with a long-term approach to investment.

Matthew Savage, Dorilton's chairman, became chairman of Williams following the acquisition alongside fellow Dorilton figure Darren Fultz and paddock insider James Matthews on the board.

This is therefore perhaps the cleanest example on the grid of our third reason for owning an F1 team.

Dorilton doesn't need Williams to sell cars, energy drinks or petrochemicals.

The racing business itself is the asset. My own conversations with Savage also make clear that this isn't simply a passive financial investment. He genuinely wants Williams to win again.

There are more layers to the corporate structure than the simple word ‘Dorilton’ suggests. The UK operating company currently records that there is no registrable person or relevant legal entity for UK PSC purposes.

This illustrates why the quality of public ownership information differs from team to team. Private investment structures, overseas entities, trusts and statutory reporting thresholds don't all produce the same neat trail.

After multiple share classes, sovereign wealth funds, private equity, holding companies, enhanced voting rights and 83-page articles of association, this comes as something of a relief.

Gene Haas founded the team.

Gene Haas controls the team.

Companies House identifies Haas as the only active person with significant control of Haas Formula UK, with 75% or more of both the shares and voting rights, Haas itself goes further, describing Gene Haas as Formula 1's only sole team owner.

That leaves Haas as the closest thing on the 2026 grid to the traditional proprietor-owned F1 team. 

How long might that last? Toyota's technical and commercial involvement with the team continues to grow and Haas has inevitably attracted investor interest as F1 valuations have increased. But as of today the ownership model remains remarkably clean and simple.

So what does an F1 owner look like in 2026?

That turned out to be a considerably longer answer than I expected.

Via different routes and structures modern F1 has accumulated different types of capital.

Racing helps another business make money.

Or you believe the racing business itself will make you money.

For much of Formula 1's history it was relatively easy to work out which box an owner belonged in.

Frank Williams wanted to win races.

Benetton wanted to sell clothes.

Renault wanted to sell cars.

Today the boxes increasingly sit on top of each other. 

Winning can now be both the sporting objective and the mechanism through which a shareholder achieves a wider commercial or investment return.

One thing that revealed itself as I dug into the detail is that an F1 team has now become valuable enough that an owner no longer necessarily must choose between keeping it and selling it.

Renault could sell 24% of Alpine, raise €200million and retain control.

Audi could bring QIA into Sauber without surrendering its works team.

Toto Wolff could sell 15% of his Mercedes ownership vehicle while retaining his role and control.

Lawrence Stroll has brought successive investors into Aston Martin while preserving overwhelming voting power.

For an owner, a multibillion dollar valuation can therefore become more than a theoretical number on a Forbes list. You can monetise part of it.

For the incoming investor the calculation is the opposite. There are only 11 F1 teams and very few owners who want to sell one.

If the only way into an appreciating global sports franchise is buying 10%, 20% or 24% while somebody else remains in charge, increasingly sophisticated investors appear perfectly happy to do that.

That is a very different Formula 1 ownership market from the one that existed even a decade ago.

How that happened and when an F1 team stopped being something you had to continually fund and became something investors fought to own is an extraordinary case study to explore.

For now, though, I started this exercise asking who is actually benefiting from the huge increase in Formula 1 team values?

The answer isn't private equity. It isn't the manufacturers. And it isn't a collection of billionaires.

Formula 1 hasn't replaced one type of owner with another.

It has become valuable enough to attract them all.

items.title: 'I f***ed it up' - Acosta explains his crash from Austria sprint lead
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The KTM rider had dominated practice, then moved from third to first on the opening lap as both Jorge Martin and Marc Marquez made errors.

Acosta was over two seconds clear of the recovering Martin with three laps to go when he then crashed at the chicane.

I was riding in a really good mood, the pace was really good, I was just checking the laps that there was remaining in the dash to see how I was with the fuelling and I f***ed it up, that's it. I lost my braking point and that's it," he explained.

Three laps to go, three seconds ahead, it also was the moment that I rolled off a bit to not take any risks and also was the moment that I lost focus a bit.

"Tomorrow, if I'm in the same place, sure, I will not roll off." 

Acosta ran into the run-off area at the chicane when he made the mistake and then fell when his KTM touched the gravel there.

Asked if there had been any chance he could have saved the incident if he hadn't tried to make the corner at all, he replied "f**k, I was that fast that it was even going to be tough to cut the corner".

He added: "Also, my mistake was not that big for the amount of speed that I was carrying. It was a mess on my side. Thankfully tomorrow we have another chance."

Acosta remounted and continued in 13th initially before retiring a lap later.

I was out of the points, I was slow, I had to warm up the tyres again. It was not necessary to take any risks," he explained when asked by The Race why he'd eventually pitted even though he still seemed competitive.

He wasn't sure if his domination of the race before the crash was a reflection of the KTM's pace or his main rivals focusing on each other, with Martin having to come back through from eighth after his first lap error.

"I was surprised that I was really fast at the beginning, that normally is where I struggle the most," said Acosta.

"And also they were having their own fight. I was just making my way."

He said his sprint error would make "zero" difference to how he approached Sunday's grand prix, when he'll again start third alongside Martin and Marquez. 

"I have nothing to lose. And also it's [the grand prix] the moment that I'm showing more speed, with more constant good results."

items.title: Martin back into MotoGP lead after Acosta throws away sprint win
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Jorge Martin came back from eighth to first after an early tussle with MotoGP title rival Marc Marquez to win the Austrian Grand Prix sprint - but only after Pedro Acosta crashed from a comfortable lead.

Polesitter Martin had gone slightly wide into the first corner at the start, allowing Marquez's Ducati to get a run on his Aprilia into the following machine.

Martin's bid to hang on as Marquez came through left him visiting the run-off area, crunching over the kerbs and losing all momentum on the exit - dropping him right back to eighth.

But Marquez then ran wide at the tight right-hander at the top of the hill, with Acosta's KTM slipping through and duly charging away.

Martin's recovery was rapid - even Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi and main title rival Marquez unable to hold him back as he sliced through to second again by half-distance.

Acosta looked out of reach, though - two and a half seconds ahead and showing no sign of being caught.

But then with three laps to go, Acosta went down going into the chicane, carrying far too much speed into the complex and losing it in the gravel trap. He got going again before soon retiring in the pits.

Martin duly swept to victory ahead of Marquez and Bezzecchi, putting him back in the championship lead by three points.

Ai Ogura marked his first race back after injury by claiming fourth via a late pass on Alex Marquez.

Pecco Bagnaia scored his first points since July's German GP in sixth, ahead of top Honda Johann Zarco, Fermin Aldguer's Gresini Ducati and final scorer Brad Binder.

items.title: Martin beats Marquez and Acosta to Austria MotoGP pole
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Jorge Martin beat MotoGP championship rival Marc Marquez and Friday dominator Pedro Acosta to a vital Austrian Grand Prix pole.

Acosta carried his immense practice form for home team KTM through to the first part of Q2 but was upstaged on the final laps by Aprilia rider Martin and Marquez's works Ducati.

Marquez and Martin share the championship lead after Marquez's pair of wins and Martin's arm pump issues at Misano last weekend, with Marquez officially ahead on countback.

Martin's team-mate Marco Bezzecchi was two tenths of a second off the front row trio in fourth, just in front of Trackhouse's post-injury returnee Ai Ogura.

Though three of the Aprilias start in the top five, the other couldn't get beyond Q1. Raul Fernandez qualified only 13th, his worst starting position since Austin six months ago.

Gresini's Alex Marquez crashed at Turn 1 in the final moments of Q2, just as brother Marc had in the final moments of the preceding practice session.

After a very poor Friday, Pecco Bagnaia made it through from Q1 along with Johann Zarco and qualified an encouraging seventh.

items.title: Gary Anderson: Four incident rule changes F1 should make
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
There’s a set of circumstances in Formula 1 that have irritated me for a long time, something the first race at the new Madring circuit last week exposed.

First of all, the use of the VSC.

Yes, it’s better than using the safety car every time a car stops on the track, but the reality is if the yellow flag or double yellow flag were adhered to by the drivers and a simple set of consistent penalties were issued, then we wouldn’t need the VSC quite so often.

However, we have got ourselves into this situation, and it is ruining racing.

There is no way Lando Norris deserved to lose that race at the Madring. He was fully in control, and just because of his on-track position, he lost out to Kimi Antonelli. Even Antonelli admitted, “It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved the win”.

Norris drove a qualifying lap that, as he says, was probably the best lap of his F1 career.

He led from pole on medium tyres and eeked out a decent gap and then at the end of lap 14, just as he passed the pit entry, the race director called for a VSC when Lance Stroll pulled off. His rivals got a cheap pitstop, while the VSC was recalled before Norris could take advantage on the next lap.

A simple change that doesn’t even require a regulation change would be that all drivers have to pass the start-finish line at least once during a VSC interlude.

This would mean that all drivers would have a chance to complete a reduced time-loss pitstop, so it would take away good or bad luck from a grand prix race result.

After all, we have something similar when the safety car is being used, the safety car pulls into the pits at the pit entry, however, drivers can’t overtake until the start-finish line.

Yes, in the end Norris may not have won the race because of other circumstances, but to potentially steal it away from him through no fault of his is basically influencing the end result.

So the question I have to ask is: when could this situation be intentionally used to manipulate a race result? It wasn’t this time, but it could be questioned if it was a close call for points near the end of a championship.

Some would say it potentially reduces racing laps, but I don’t agree. If we look at this situation at the Madring, it would have meant we would have stayed under the VSC for another 20 seconds, so it's no big deal.

Also another thing that bugs me is that when a red flag is thrown during qualifying, the driver who causes the red flag doesn’t really suffer any setback, other than perhaps a damaged car, but drivers on a quick lap potentially lose a set of tyres by having to abort their lap.

Why can’t the red flag be thrown from the start-finish line to the scene of the incident? Drivers on a qualifying lap that is past the scene of the incident could finish their lap.

Also, if the medical car was required, it could exit the pits at the end of the pitlane so well into the red flag area of the track.

Yes cars between the start-finish line and the scene of the incident would still lose a set of tyres, but it’s the old saying: you can’t please all of the people all of the time, but at least you could potentially please some of the drivers some of the time.

As far as the driver who causes a red flag getting a penalty, in F2 any driver who causes a red flag loses all their qualifying laps. Personally, I think that is a bit heavy-handed, but to lose your fastest lap in that qualifying session would be a fair punishment. It could make the difference between getting into the next qualifying session or even your actual grid position if you caused it in the final session.

Also, during a race red flag situation, I don’t think that drivers should be able to change tyre compounds, so basically you can’t comply with the two-compound race requirement.

Yes, you can change tyres to reduce the risk of tyre damage or punctures from running over debris, but that would be the same for everyone. So it again reduces the potential influence on the race result for those who have pitted prior to the red flag and those who hadn’t.

items.title: What we learned at Red Bull and Verstappen's wild kart race
items.author: Megan Cantle
items.content:
There was just one question on everyone's lips at Silverstone on Wednesday evening: could Max Verstappen beat 100 karters when starting from the very back of the grid?

The answer, emphatically, was yes.

Max vs 100 was the latest in a long-line of incredible marketing stunts from Red Bull, bringing together athletes, creators and journalists to take on the four-time Formula 1 world champion. The catch? He'd be starting from 101st and would be tasked with picking off every single one of them around the extended karting track at Silverstone.

Opinions were mixed on whether he'd be able to do it, with Arvid Lindblad having put the two halves of the grid through their paces the day before. He'd had less time to do it in, but was beaten in the first race, leading people to question whether Verstappen - with twice as many competitors and plenty of opportunities for pile-ups and chaos - would get it done in time.

That line of questioning was rendered redundant when he passed 60-plus people on the opening lap, and went on to win the race in just 14 of the planned 30 laps, even with a slight excursion that might have raised some track-limits eyebrows in an F1 race.

Impressive as that was, what was really astonishing was how many moving parts were constantly at play during the lead-up and race day itself.

The 100 karters were made up of some who had never even sat in one before alongside drivers with some serious experience and speed. They were given proper training and acclimatisation time and, even if some of them were "bounced past" before they had even taken the first corner, they were all brought up to speed remarkably quickly to a safe and competent level.

Red Bull really made the most of the event, and it was clear from his post-race press conference that Verstappen had genuinely enjoyed himself. Karting is the purest form of racing and no matter how much F1 experience a driver has, you can tell they all enjoy returning to it. It was never 'gimmicky' even though there were 'gimmicks', with the newly created proximity chat proving a hit with both the audience and seemingly Verstappen himself. (An F1 introduction when?)

As part of a group of media invited to the event, it's hard to quite put into words how much fun it was. We had access to the host of karters, a chance to put some questions to driver-trainer extraordinaire Lindblad, plus dinner and a tour at Red Bull's MK7 campus. You could tell there was a lot of genuine care and thought put into all of the details and, given the amount of people involved, it was remarkable that everything ran so smoothly.

Some parties involved in the running of the event might have hoped the race would have lasted a little longer, but all that means is that they'll have to give it another go at some point in the future. Anyone up for Max vs 200?

items.title: MotoGP Austrian GP: Who made Q2 - and who missed out
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Pedro Acosta continued to command KTM and Red Bull's home MotoGP race as he led throughout the Austrian Grand Prix Friday afternoon practice session too.

Gresini Ducati rider Fermin Aldeguer ended up his closest challenger, 0.127 seconds adrift.

Ai Ogura marked his return to the field after hand surgery by being top Aprilia in an impressive third place for Trackhouse.

None of the title contenders showed especially standout pace, though Marc Marquez brought his Ducati up to fourth by the end, just ahead of Jorge Martin's Aprilia.

Martin's team-mate Marco Bezzecchi had a particularly muted Friday, bar some errors under braking, and was only ninth.

The session was interrupted by a late red flag for a nasty crash for Alex Marquez.

His Gresini Ducati's front wheel locked as it hit the ground from a small wheelie out of the first corner, firing him into a crash that sent him sliding down the straight while his bike cartwheeled down the grass.

Marquez was able to rejoin on his spare bike after the restart and earned a Q2 place in eighth, just behind an unusually strong late-2026 performance from outgoing KTM rider Brad Binder.

Yamaha will be represented in Q2 thanks to Fabio Quartararo taking 10th place.

But Honda missed out despite LCR's Johann Zarco spending much of the afternoon in the top 10.

Zarco had an early crash at Turn 4 in which team-mate Diogo Moreira also went through the gravel while he was walking away. The stewards quickly determined that Moreira had had no time to react so had not breached yellow flag rules.

The LCR pair were edged down to 12th and 13th at the end, just behind works Honda rider Luca Marini.

items.title: KTM CEO reveals Acosta's key Marquez stance for 2027
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
KTM CEO Gottfried Neumeister says there was no financial offer that KTM could have made to tempt Pedro Acosta to stay, because Acosta is desperate to measure himself against Marc Marquez.

Though Acosta is yet to win a grand prix, he and Marquez are the two arguable standouts of the current campaign - with Marquez now the title favourite despite injury troubles and Acosta massively outperforming his KTM peers.

Acosta agreed a deal to replace Pecco Bagnaia at Ducati in the last off-season - despite the widespread belief that he could have commanded more lucrative contracts elsewhere.

KTM motorsport boss Pit Beirer said last weekend that KTM felt "there was somehow a chance" to kept him - "but also it was quite long growing in him that he wanted to go there and have the same bike as Marc, and just find out who is better, him or Marc, so there's something I think we couldn't even beat".

And this was corroborated emphatically by Neumeister during KTM's home MotoGP weekend at the Red Bull Ring, when he was asked by The Race about the damage losing Acosta does to his brand's championship ambitions in the short-term in MotoGP.

Neumeister was very keen to emphasise his faith in KTM's future factory line-up of Alex Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - also making a point to specifically mention it after the end of his media session.

But of Acosta leaving, he said: "I'm really very sorry, and I tried. And it's not a secret. I tried personally to convince him to stay.

"But I mean, I still have goosebumps because he told me, 'Listen, Gottfried, it's not about a million more or less'.

"We have seen riders who are sitting on the best bike at the beginning of the season just signing with others for money. This is, for me, not a racing spirit, yeah?

"And he simply said: 'I'm Spanish. Even if you have a better bike, the 850cc, and I'd be winning on this one, I want to beat Marc with the same weapon.'

"And then you're disarmed, you're dismantled. And this is such a great encouragement. And I will always have the best feelings when I see him."

The line about 'signing with others for money' can be read as reference to joint-championship leader Jorge Martin - who had left KTM on bad terms half a decade ago and who this year committed to a switch from Aprilia to Yamaha early on.

All the evidence corroborates Neumeister's suggestion that KTM's relationship with Acosta remains very healthy until their end-of-year separation - with Acosta allowed to again test KTM's 850cc prototype this Monday at the Red Bull Ring (he already tested it at Brno) and Neumeister making reference to a potential reunion down the line.

items.title: Senior TT moved from Isle of Man finale slot in 2027 changes
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
The Isle of Man TT has announced schedule changes for 2027 that will concentrate race-week activities around the blue riband Senior TT event, partly as a response to weather disruptions in recent years.

The new schedule also sees one race dropped from the calendar, with the Superstock class reduced to just a single race - something that happened in 2026 anyway when the second race was scrapped due to the inclement weather that disrupted most of race week after glorious sunshine during practice week.

The Superbike TT, traditionally the opening race of the event, will reclaim that slot for 2027 after swapping with the first Supersport race for 2026, with the four-lap Supersport TT now taking its place on Sunday with its shorter, closed-roads window thanks to the island's church services.

Monday will be a contingency day, ahead of the Superstock TT on Tuesday and the return of the sidecar class following its 2026 suspension on safety grounds, with the second Supersport TT and the newly revamped Sportbike TT class going on Wednesday.

Thursday will be another rest day, with only the Senior TT scheduled for Friday (traditionally a public holiday on the Isle of Man). This year's race was rescheduled for Saturday and was due to be shortened to four laps, but could not be completed due to rain and windy conditions - meaning the result was taken from the single lap of racing completed before a red flag the previous evening.

Racing will then conclude on Saturday with another sidecar race and the second Sportbike race.

"The schedule introduced in 2023 achieved a number of important objectives for the TT," said TT boss Paul Phillips. "It created stronger opening and closing weekends, provided more racing across the week and gave visitors much greater choice around how and when they came to the Island.

"Across the four TT events in which it has operated, the schedule has helped us attract more fans and deliver greater economic benefit to the island. Those gains remain central to the 2027 programme, but four years of experience have also provided valuable evidence about where the schedule can now be refined.

"For 2027, we believe the right balance is nine substantial and clearly defined races. Moving from two Superstock races to one allows us to give the remaining Superstock race and both Sportbike races greater substance, create more recovery time within the programme and provide better protection around the Superbike and Senior TTs.

"This is an evolution rather than a return to the programme that existed before 2023. It retains the stronger two-weekend structure while giving each race day a clear purpose. Superbike provides an immediate headline race on the opening Saturday, while placing the 100th Senior on Friday allows us to build the day around that historic occasion and retain Saturday as a genuine contingency opportunity.

"We also want the 100th Senior to be about much more than the race itself. It gives us an opportunity to celebrate the riders, motorcycles and extraordinary performances that have made it the most important race at the TT."

2027 Isle of Man TT race schedule

Superbike TT - 6 laps

Supersport TT Race 1 - 4 laps

Contingency day

Superstock TT - 4 laps

Sidecar TT Race 1 - 2 laps

Supersport TT Race 2 - 4 laps

Sportbike TT Race 1 - 4 laps

Contingency day

Senior TT - 6 laps

Sidecar TT Race 2 - 2 laps

Sportbike TT Race 2 - 4 laps

items.title: Where the next leaps in F1 brake technology will come from
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
"Probably the only thing that is in common is that it has carbon as a chemical element. The rest is completely different."

That's how Mario Almondo, Chief Officer of Brembo Performance, describes how Formula 1 brakes of 2026 compare to what was used 20 years earlier. And the next 20 years could bring even bigger changes - though not necessarily in materials.

It's in the last 10 years in particular that Almondo feels visitors to Brembo's factory in Curno, Italy, have been overwhelmed by what goes into F1 brake design and creation "in terms of energy, complexity and the variety of processes behind the creation of the material that makes up an F1 brake".

"You have to create the material, it's not like melting a cast iron disc," he adds of carbon.

Over the last two decades, that process has changed radically.

"It is completely different in terms of shapes and quality of the rotors and their lay-up, as well as the design and cooling of the brake pads," says Almondo.

"It is completely different in terms of the cycle of production into the furnaces. The cycle time is even more different. We also had some different chemical and thermodynamics reactions, let's say, compared to even the recent past, we are using improved gas mixtures.

"It is different in terms of the additives and chemical additives that we put onto the discs and pads. 

"The process of manufacturing is completely different, because, of course, we started with 50 holes or something like that. Now, we are at more than 1000.

"As I said, the chemical element of carbon is still there, but that's it!"

Brembo is about to introduce carbon-ceramic brakes into superbike racing, a project that’s been in progress for more than five years in terms of what Almondo calls "the cooking recipe" of the creation of the brakes by maximising thermal, mechanical, and friction profile properties.

While that is now sufficient to slow a high-performance racing bike, Almondo (above) believes F1-level braking - "the best expression of the technology in terms of pure performance" - will still require all carbon-carbon brakes for "several years still" because the friction level, resistance and thermal properties achievable with carbon-ceramic discs is not at that level required from F1 cars.

So while a major material change might not be on the immediate horizon for F1 brakes, the big leap Almondo foresees is around how "digitally pre-empted" the braking group can be, before it even gets on an F1 car. Simulation tools aren't just helping F1 teams, they're a massive boost for suppliers such as Brembo too - achieving remarkable results in the preparation and anticipation of problems that may arise with any new project, such as the implementation of the new technical regulations at the start of 2026.

"You have to digitalise and simulate everything and you have to foresee what's going to happen. And this is something where we are very, very, very good," says Almondo.

"For example, this year, there are completely new technical rules in Formula 1. It is something that I'm very proud of that if I have to compare what we predicted and what was happening at the first test or the first race this year, we were 99% spot on."

And asked where the next technical advances in F1 braking were most likely to come, it's in this area of simulation that Almondo expects the biggest strides.

"Probably, simulation is the area where we have more room for expansion and the quickest pace of expansion, because the rest is linked to something that is more physical," he explains.

"And of course, physics has to be tested, proved, retested. It is a constant pace, but not with big leaps.

"While on the other side, with simulation, if you have a good idea, you can find something that gives you the possibility and room for big expansion and big low-cost improvement - indeed, digitally validating a new idea drastically shortens development times, even though physical component testing must still be carried out."

The level of complexity in a 2026 F1 braking system, especially in terms of blending with the regenerative braking component, it remains a highly demanding engineering challenge.

"The reason why I say 'braking technology', because it is not just about calipers and other mechanical components, but it's also about software, it's about simulation, it's about brake-by-wire, it's about the pump and all this kind of stuff. It is very, very complex, the interaction between the vehicle and the braking technology," explains Almondo.

And it's in this area of interaction between the braking system and the wider car performance that Almondo thinks most competitive gains can be made in the coming years.

"The evolution will be towards having a technology of braking that is much more into the dynamic of the car, much more interacting with the dynamic of the car, because of course this is better for the packaging," he says. 

"This is what everybody is asking, and this is because it is the natural way to better integrate the dissipative braking with the regenerative braking - through software, through technology, through hydraulics, through electrical.

"It's something that is completely in evolution and we rely on this kind of development, we rely as well on the input of the teams. We are here for this."

The likelihood of the next generation of F1 regulations being simpler - with a smaller electrical energy component potentially teamed with a V8 internal combustion engine - does appeal to Almondo personally, but he warns against regarding it as a simpler challenge for braking technology.

"Of course, braking with an ICE is something that we know very well, but the point is that you have to go to the limit and a little bit above the limit, but keeping performance and, of course, safety at 100%," he says.

"So, if we go in this direction, we are going to play on a pitch that we know very well - and that I like, I have to say also personally, in terms of a motorsport exercise. And in any case, it certainly seems to be the direction that the vast number of F1 fans are asking for."

"But it will always be the same: constant improvement, we will reach the limit, some teams will, as usual, push us to overtake the limit a little bit, because they want more, more, more, and this is why Brembo is what it is."

And wherever F1 car technology goes, braking performance is going to be critical to it.

As Almondo puts it: "Ifyou want to have something rolling, of course, you have to have something to stop it. That’s been true since the invention of the wheel!"

items.title: What happened in KTM-led first Austria MotoGP practice
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
KTM started it and title sponsor Red Bull's home MotoGP weekend with a 1-2 in opening Austrian Grand Prix practice.

Pedro Acosta - who would particularly like to win his first full MotoGP grand prix in Austria as he goes into his final months with KTM before leaving for Ducati - set an early 1m29.851s that kept him on top.

Tech3's Maverick Vinales stand-in Pol Espargaro then used fresh tyres at the end to go to second, just over two tenths of a second slower, as he recovered from an early crash.

Joint championship leader Jorge Martin had to switch to his spare Aprilia after a technical problem in the opening minutes, but was second until Espargaro's late run.

Martin is optimistic that the nature of the Red Bull Ring layout will mean there is no repeat of the arm pump problem that caused his Misano slump last weekend and allowed Marc Marquez to draw level with him in the championship and lead on countback.

Marquez was fourth in the session, with fellow title contender Marco Bezzecchi sixth behind top Honda rider Johann Zarco.

Alex Marquez fell back to eighth in the final minutes having been in the top five but run through the gravel after part of the aero on his Gresini Ducati came loose.

items.title: Do driving styles really explain these drivers' 2026 F1 struggles?
items.author: Mark Hughes
items.content:
After two sectors in the final Q3 runs of Madring George Russell was within 0.1 seconds of Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli. By the end of the lap, he’d dropped a further two tenths. An average of half-a-tenth loss in the first two sectors but four times that in the last one.

His rear tyres were simply too hot for the repeated 90-degree turns of sector three and that, obviously, was a function of how he had used them up to that point.

It defined his weekend as one in which he finished fifth, half-a-minute adrift of the race-winning Antonelli, albeit on a different strategy.

It was somehow emblematic of Russell's 2026 season, probably the weakest of his eight-year F1 career at just the time he finally gets a title-calibre car. 

Afterwards he was pondering where his struggles this year lay and he puts it firmly in the category of a mismatch between his natural driving style and the demands of the 2026 generation of car and tyre.

"It's been a strange season when you look at the competitiveness of [Oscar] Piastri against Lando [Norris] last year, Charles [Leclerc] versus Lewis [Hamilton] and even the dominance of Max [Verstappen] against all of his team-mates in the previous era," Russell said.

"This year myself, Charles, Oscar are struggling much more compared to our team-mates. And Max, his team-mates have been substantially closer to him than anybody has in the last six years, and I think we've all got pretty similar driving styles.

"The drivers performing very well this year - Kimi, Lewis, Lando - have got quite similar driving styles. So to me it's pretty clear with this car, with these tyres, the trends are there."

There is almost certainly a causal relationship between these cars/tyres and the struggles of Russell and Piastri. They each tend to drive to a geometric ideal, late turn-in with a positively abrupt initial turn of the wheel, relying more on that steering than weight manipulation for rotation into the turn and using very little overlap between braking and cornering.

It can work brilliantly well on a high-grip track in a car with a lot of downforce. But not as well as the grip reduces.

Get more in-depth F1 driving style analysis from Mark Hughes and Edd Straw in their series in The Race Members' Club

The reduced downforce and tyre grip of the 2026 cars has raised the crossover point of circuit grip at which that technique begins to be problematic - ie with these cars there are more circuits than before which don't really sync very well with that technique.  

Furthermore, the penalty of that is compounded in these cars by the demands of energy management. The less momentum you can maintain on entry, the more in-fills the battery makes, meaning the deployment doesn't last as long on the straights. Russell and Piastri have both struggled in places with this. 

But the equivalence Russell makes breaks down when comparing Verstappen and Leclerc, who each have their own styles unrelated to each other's or those of Russell and Piastri.

Verstappen has perhaps the most versatile range of skills of anyone on the grid, but his preference is a car with an extreme front end which allows him to derive corner rotation from relatively little steering. He has the amazing sensitivity to rotation and yaw, which allows him to adjust steering/brakes/throttle to dampen out the latent exit oversteer which would normally come with an 'on-the-nose' car.

Any car - such as the current Red Bull RB22 - which understeers at low- and medium-speed entries will limit how much laptime that skill buys him over others. The performance profile of other cars suggests that it's perfectly feasible to have an on-the-nose car under these regulations. It's just that Red Bull has not been able to provide one. 

Leclerc has traditionally got his rotation from an energetic balancing act between brakes/throttle/steering, with lots of overlap. It makes him absolutely dynamite around short corners where the reward for the quick rotation isn't overwhelmed by the penalty later in the corner.

He's probably the fastest driver there is around Monaco, Baku and the Red Bull Ring. But long-corner tracks - Shanghai, Hungaroring - can present difficulties for him, as a price is extracted later in the corner for the way he tricked the car into turning more than it wanted initially. The 2026 regulation's demand for energy management mean that some of those tricks have become almost redundant. But he remains a fantastically fast driver. 

Antonelli, Norris and Hamilton are also quite distinctive in their styles - and adaptable.

In fact, Hamilton's adaptation to the demands of this generation of car after his struggles with the ground-effect era has been one of the most noteworthy driver performance stories of the season.

As a generalisation, he keeps the car flatter and calmer than Leclerc on entry and this means there is a variance in corner type at which one betters the other. He's still able to be super-late on the brakes when required, but he's combining it with a suppleness that is not overworking the front axle - and the Ferrari's downforce balance is allowing that to work very well for him. 

Antonelli and Norris have clearly worked very hard with their engineering teams to understand the quirks of these cars as they've introduced features in their driving specifically tuned to the energy management. Antonelli's throttle usage is highly distinctive, for example, and seems to be tailored around maximising harvest under braking rather than wasting it on part-throttle.

His inputs are beautifully smooth as he judges the grip upon entry with such precision and confidence that there is very little corrective input required through the corner - this is probably the most visible contrast between him and Russell.

It suggests he's just got a better feel for the front-axle grip, but when the grip is high he's perfectly comfortable taking the Russell late entry/big steering approach. He just seems to have a better awareness of when that's not the optimum tactic. 

Get exclusive Mark Hughes insight direct to your inbox every week with his The Long Run newsletter -

Norris has always had a beautiful way of progressively loading the front of the car up and can take whatever line is needed according to the available grip.

As with Verstappen, it's a style which tends to fall apart if the car is an understeerer, but using that progression, sometimes turning in shallow from further back (seen to great effect in the final turn at the Hungaroring in FP1 when the grip was super-low), means he suffers far less from snaps on the exit, because he doesn't have as much lock on when the fronts finally grip. 

Norris himself doesn't see his style as the distinctive differentiator.

"I wouldn't really say my driving style suits this car," he says. "I think my driving style is good because I'm able to adapt better. I don't think it's one style that works and I don't drive the same way as Kimi…my adaptability is what allows me to drive the car I've got. My strength is my adaptability to different driving styles. 

"Last year at the beginning [the car] suited Oscar a little bit more. My strength was being able to adapt better to then finally understand how to drive it in a better way. Hence I had a better second half of the season. 

"This year? You don't drive this car anywhere close to last year, not even 1% I feel is remotely the same. So it’s about adaptation."

The bottom line is Russell (and Piastri) have to adapt. Because the cars aren't coming to them.

items.title: 'It looks terrible' - Bagnaia infuriated by Di Giannantonio chat airing
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Pecco Bagnaia says he has been made to look "terrible" by the airing of a conversation with Ducati MotoGP stablemate Fabio Di Giannantonio, which he believes was taken out of context.

Footage released by Spanish broadcaster DAZN, captured at Misano between various broadcaster interviews as Di Giannantonio semi-privately quizzed Bagnaia about his struggles with the bike, picked up a lot of steam online due to one particular phrase by Bagnaia - a suggestion that Ducati "isn't letting" him use a more straightforward set-up.

Bagnaia fully anticipated questions about this coming into Thursday at the Red Bull Ring - and said that while he regretted his "not correct" phrasing, he also clearly felt he was treated unfairly by DAZN.

"You know me very well, you listen to me every day when we are racing," Bagnaia told the assembled print journalists. "I think that many times it was asked to me: 'Is the team supporting you?'

"And I always said yes, the team is doing the maximum to help me.

"The video that was out of recording was out of context [...] The video is not complete. We were speaking about one more thing [specific part].

"Sometimes you say things in the wrong way. But what I always said is that Ducati supported me a lot - and what I meant is that I tried to put and remove [certain parts] many times already, so Ducati is not allowing me to do [it] anymore. But just because I already did many times - and I don't want to continue this kind of thing. What came out of my mouth was [said] in the wrong way.

"But then what happened next is a disaster for me. Because it's completely out of [devoid of] respect. And the relationship between journalists and riders needs respect.

"Yesterday we spoke about it [within Ducati]. It's normal that, the way it comes out on television, it looks terrible."

The footage has since been erased by DAZN, which has apologised to Bagnaia - who said Ducati understood the situation and "know that I'm not completely crazy".

"It's clear that you can take our words and put them online in the way you want. Because you can say three words and can have two different complete contexts. Positive or negative. 

"You [media] are the ones that need to be transparent, and understand what we are saying. But I know that sometimes it's important to have a nice clickbait title.

"But I always try to be as transparent as possible. But I will try to be less. In the future maybe you will have less from me."

Di Giannantonio, who ended up an unwitting third party in the controversy, was also displeased on Bagnaia's behalf.

"I don't want to say something about this story [specifically] because it's not my story, but I can say that us as riders, especially us as Italians, we have known each other for a long time - and we always talk about bikes, it's completely normal for us. What happened, it was a thing outside the cameras, but apparently it was inside. So I think it was a bit unfair [to air it].

"But the problem is now that we always have cameras - so we are going to a world where we cannot talk anymore.

"Journalists should have a sense of limit. It's like, I can be in a pub talking about bikes and I don't have to be worried that somewhere there is a journalist with a mic, because it was a friendly chat.

"For sure it's a thing that we can improve as a sport, also because I think it's not nice for the sport, honestly."

As for his specific conversation with Bagnaia, Di Giannantonio said he was keen to offer his advice to Bagnaia because he had benefitted from the works Ducati's rider input in the past.

"When I was struggling with the Ducati, I was always talking with Pecco and trying to get as much info as I can, and he was always helping me, trying to give me the best advice to improve - and when I can, I try to do the same with other riders that I have known for a long time. So it was a completely normal chat for us."

items.title: Hamilton firmly denies asking for Ferrari staff to be replaced
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Ferrari Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton has taken to social media to insist he’s “never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced” after a report in the Italian media suggested he had. 

Italian newspaper Corriere della Seraclaimed Hamilton had asked for changes to be made to trackside personnel at Ferrari and reported a weakened relationship with team boss Fred Vasseur, who had been instrumental to Hamilton signing in the first place. 

But on Thursday, Hamilton posted an Instagram story that rubbished the rumours.

“I’ve seen some of the stories that have gone out and I want to clear it up here. I’ve never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced,” Hamilton wrote.

“Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward. 

“I always try to empower and lift people to be the best versions of themselves or at least see the best in themselves. 

“I may not always achieve that but it’s my intention and that’s what I’m here to do. 

“We all work together and that will continue.” 

It follows a tricky patch for Ferrari, which hasn’t had a grand prix podium since Spa in July.
